flashcards.q: What is the difference between node --inspect and node --inspect-brk?
flashcards.a: --inspect starts the process running immediately, attach anytime, missing anything before attach. --inspect-brk pauses on the very first line and won't proceed until a debugger connects -- needed for module-load-time bugs.

flashcards.q: Why can dlv attach <pid> connect to an unmodified running Go binary while Node's inspector and Java's JDWP cannot?
flashcards.a: Delve's attach uses ptrace directly at the OS level, needing no prior instrumentation. Node's inspector and JDWP are runtime-level protocols requiring the process to open a listening port at startup via a flag, which can't be retrofitted onto an already-running process.

flashcards.q: What does suspend=y vs suspend=n control in a JDWP connection string?
flashcards.a: suspend=y blocks the JVM at startup until a debugger actually attaches, running no application code (catches static-init/class-load bugs). suspend=n lets the JVM run immediately with the JDWP port simply available for later attach.

flashcards.q: How do you run Python post-mortem debugging on a script that already crashed?
flashcards.a: python -m pdb -c continue crashing_script.py runs it under pdb and drops into an interactive session at the exact frame of the unhandled exception. Interactively, pdb.pm() enters the debugger on the most recent traceback.

flashcards.q: What does PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 do and why should it be a standing production environment variable?
flashcards.a: It disables every breakpoint() call process-wide. Without it, a stray breakpoint() left in code ships to production and hangs a request indefinitely waiting on stdin that will never arrive.

flashcards.q: What does rust-gdb add over plain gdb for debugging a Rust binary?
flashcards.a: It auto-loads Rust-specific pretty-printer scripts, so enums/generics like Option::Some(42) print as their actual value instead of raw memory layout (a discriminant tag plus a union of variant data) that plain gdb has no built-in understanding of.

flashcards.q: In delve, what commands do you use to investigate a suspected goroutine deadlock?
flashcards.a: goroutines to list all goroutines and their state/location, then goroutine <id> bt to backtrace a specific blocked one, cross-referencing stacks to find the lock-ordering or channel-direction mismatch.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a watchpoint and a breakpoint, and when is a watchpoint the right tool?
flashcards.a: A breakpoint triggers at a specific line/location regardless of state. A watchpoint triggers whenever a specific variable's value changes, regardless of where in the code. Use a watchpoint when you know WHAT value became wrong but not WHERE it's being corrupted.

flashcards.q: Why is IntelliJ's "Evaluate Expression" risky against a shared staging/production JVM?
flashcards.a: It can invoke arbitrary methods on live objects including ones with real side effects (mutating state, network calls, DB writes) -- not read-only inspection, an actual production-affecting action, easy to trigger accidentally on something that looks like a harmless getter.

flashcards.q: Why does dlv attach fail inside a Kubernetes pod with a permissions error, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Delve's ptrace-based attach requires CAP_SYS_PTRACE, stripped by most container security policies by default. Fix: add securityContext.capabilities.add: [SYS_PTRACE] to the specific container temporarily, or use an ephemeral debug container (kubectl debug --target) sharing the pod's PID namespace instead.
